messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is a 35-year-old married man who works as a tax consultant. Three years ago, he spent six months as a relief worker in a conflict zone in southern Asia, where his team was responsible for distributing food and medical supplies to displaced families. One afternoon, a mortar shell struck the warehouse he was working in. He remembers the deafening blast, the ceiling collapsing, and the thick, acrid smoke that filled his lungs as he dragged two injured colleagues outside. One of them died in his arms. The other lost a leg. What haunts Rajan most is that he could not save them both. He replays the moment he chose who to pull first, and the sequence of events has become so jumbled in his mind that he is no longer certain whether his decision was even the right one. When memories surface, his body locks into the same position he was in that day — crouched, arms extended, shoulders braced — and he feels a wave of shame so sharp it leaves him breathless. He has come to believe that he failed, that he should have done more, and that this failure defines who he is.

In the months that followed, Rajan found that certain smells could undo him entirely. A neighbor lighting a charcoal grill, or the scent of smoke drifting from a kitchen, would send him retreating into his home with his hands pressed over his face. He began avoiding funerals and cemeteries, even when a close friend’s mother passed away. More puzzling to him — and more troubling to his wife — was his growing avoidance of anything that might make him feel happy. He stopped celebrating birthdays, declined invitations to dinners, and turned away from his wife when she tried to share good news. Joy felt dangerous, as though allowing himself even a moment of hope would invite another catastrophe. He was certain that the world was not a place where good things lasted, and that anyone who believed otherwise was simply naive. This belief made him feel profoundly isolated from others, even from his wife, who could not understand why he seemed to push away every moment of warmth.

Rajan’s vigilance became a constant companion. He found it harder to feel safe at night, lying awake and listening for sounds that might signal danger. Ordinary noises — a car backfiring, a door slamming — made him jump, his heart pounding as though the mortar had just landed. This hyperarousal bled into his work as a tax consultant, where he struggled to concentrate on spreadsheets and deadlines. Every time he startled, the memory of the warehouse returned with renewed force, and the shame followed, tightening the loop. He began to notice that the more isolated he felt, the more attuned he became to potential threats. A colleague’s calm expression of frustration in a meeting would trigger a cascade of panic, and Rajan would find himself covering his face with his hands, overwhelmed by the conviction that anger was a precursor to violence.

Over time, his strategies for managing these intrusions only deepened the problem. Avoiding smoke and anger meant he could no longer visit certain parts of the city or attend team meetings without preemptive anxiety. Hiding his face became a reflex, one that his colleagues began to notice and comment on. The more he avoided positive events, the more his wife withdrew, and the more isolated he became. That isolation fed his belief that he was fundamentally different from others — broken, marked by a failure they could never understand. And that belief, in turn, made him more sensitive to triggers, more vigilant, and more likely to retreat into the disordered memory of that afternoon.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment at his desk, when a client mentioned in passing that they had been to a funeral that morning. Rajan felt his chest tighten, his body locked into that crouched position, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stood with his hands over his face, shaking. His wife had told him she could not keep living this way. He is afraid that therapy will force him to relive the day he failed, but he is more afraid of losing the life he still has.
